title: Figma Live Collaboration
summary: Multiplayer design editing: each file is loaded into an authoritative in-memory server process, clients send property-level changes over WebSockets, conflicts resolve last-writer-wins per property, and periodic checkpoints plus a write-ahead journal make it durable.

head: Type
Requirement
rows: Many people edit the same design file live; see cursors, selections and changes instantly
Comments, version history, components shared across files (libraries)
Works in the browser with large files (thousands of layers)
Local edits apply instantly; remote edits visible < 100–200 ms
All clients converge; no lost work on server crash

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Per-file traffic is small. The design hinges on choosing a conflict model simpler than text OT, because design documents are trees of objects with properties.

items: A file is a tree of objects (frames, rectangles, text) each with an ID and a map of properties (x, y, fill, parent, index).
Changes are property-level: `{objectId, property, value}`.
Ordering among siblings uses fractional indexing (a string between neighbours' positions) so concurrent inserts don't collide.
Rendering engine is C++ compiled to WebAssembly drawing with WebGL in the browser.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Most design conflicts are two people setting the same property of the same object — last-writer-wins per property resolves them predictably, so full text-style OT isn't needed.

blocks.caption: One authoritative multiplayer process per open file

items: Opening a file routes all clients to the server process that owns it; that process loads the latest checkpoint + journal.
Client applies its change locally immediately and sends it.
Server applies changes in arrival order (LWW per property), acks the sender and broadcasts to others.
Client keeps unacknowledged local changes on top, so a remote change to the same property doesn't flicker over the user's own pending value.
Changes are appended to a journal for durability; the server checkpoints the whole file periodically to object storage.

head: Case
Resolution
rows: Two users set the same property
Server order decides; last write wins
Two users set different properties of one object
One deletes an object another edits
Delete wins; edits to a missing object dropped (undo can restore)
Server rejects the move that would create a cycle
Fractional index keys keep both, in a deterministic order

blocks.text: This is CRDT-inspired but server-authoritative: the central server gives a single order, which keeps the logic simple, while fractional indexing and per-property LWW behave like CRDT registers.

items: Write-ahead journal of changes (Figma moved this into a dedicated store so a server crash loses nothing acknowledged).
Checkpoints every N seconds/changes to S3; load = checkpoint + replay journal tail.
Multiplayer servers are stateful: route by file ID; if a server dies, the file reopens on another server from checkpoint + journal and clients reconnect.
Viewers (read-only) can be served by fan-out replicas so a 'company all-hands' file doesn't overload one process.
Presence (cursors, selections) is ephemeral, throttled (~30 Hz) and never journaled.
Client tracks the last acknowledged sequence; on reconnect it receives changes since then and re-sends unacknowledged local changes.
Brief offline edits survive and merge by the same LWW rules; long offline sessions may need a full reload.
Undo is per user: inverse of the user's own changes, applied as new changes.

head: Failure
Impact
Mitigation
rows: Reload on new server from checkpoint + journal; clients resend pending
Lazy load pages, incremental checkpoints, binary format
Lease on file ownership with fencing on journal writes

items.title: Requirements
items.text: Live multiplayer design editing, history, comments.

items.title: Model
items.text: Object tree with property maps; fractional indexing.

items.title: HLD
items.text: Router → multiplayer server per file → journal + checkpoints.

items.title: Wrap-up
items.text: Hot files, crash recovery, latency metrics.

items.q: Why not OT like Google Docs?
items.a: Design docs aren't linear text; property-level LWW plus tree rules is simpler and covers nearly all real conflicts. Text layers can still use finer merging.

items.q: How do shared component libraries update?
items.a: Library publishes a version; consuming files get an update notification and pull new component definitions as changes.
Checkpoints become restorable versions; named versions are pinned checkpoints.

items: File = tree of objects with property maps.
Server-authoritative, last-writer-wins per property.
Fractional indexing for sibling order.
Client keeps pending local changes on top until acked.
Journal + checkpoints for durability.
Presence ephemeral and throttled.
